title: Reversible and irreversible processes
summary: A reversible change can be undone exactly; a sudden, real one cannot, and some work is wasted as heat.
alt: A gas expanded and compressed either slowly or suddenly with a P–V graph: the slow path retraces itself and the sudden path encloses a wasted-work area.

steps.title: Can the gas go back exactly?
steps.text: We will expand a gas from **A to B** and then compress it back. If the gas **and** the surroundings both return exactly to where they began, the process is **reversible**.

steps.title: Slow expansion and return
steps.text: Done **very slowly**, the gas is almost in equilibrium at every moment, so it follows the same curve out and back. Nothing is wasted: the process is **reversible**.

steps.title: Sudden expansion and return
steps.text: Now do it **suddenly**: the pressure drops at once and the piston flies out; to return, the pressure is raised at once. The path out and back are **different**.

steps.title: The wasted work
steps.text: The loop between the two paths is the **work wasted as heat**. The surroundings cannot be restored: the process is **irreversible**. Real processes always are.

steps.title: Everyday irreversible processes
steps.text: Friction, heat flowing from hot to cold, a gas rushing into a vacuum, and mixing milk into tea are all **irreversible**. None of them ever runs backwards by itself.

formulas.title: Reversible process
formulas.tex: \text{gas and surroundings can both be restored exactly}
formulas.text: Only possible if the process is infinitely slow with no friction and no heat flow across a temperature difference.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: Which of these is closest to a **reversible** process?

options.label: A gas compressed very slowly while kept in thermal equilibrium
A gas rushing into a vacuum
A hot cup cooling in a cold room
A brake pad rubbing a wheel

challenges.explain: Only extremely slow changes with no friction or heat flow across a temperature difference are (nearly) reversible.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: Heat flowing from a hot body to a cold body is:
challenges.hint: Have you ever seen it flow back by itself?
challenges.explain: It never reverses by itself: it is irreversible.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: In the sudden expansion and return, the loop on the P–V graph represents:
challenges.hint: The area of the loop is net work.
challenges.explain: The enclosed area is work that was done on the gas and not recovered: it ended up as heat in the surroundings.

takeaways: A **reversible** process can be undone so that both the system and surroundings return to their original states.
**All real processes are irreversible** (friction, heat flow, rapid expansion).
The **Carnot engine** is built from reversible processes: it is an ideal limit.

notes.title: Connects to
notes.text: Irreversibility is the idea behind the **second law** and **entropy**: natural processes go one way only. The Carnot engine is the reversible ideal that gives the maximum efficiency.
